body.statement: If \(P\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\geq1\) and \(\det G_P\equiv0\) in \(\mathbb R[S3]\), then symmetry of the second derivative gives \(\mathrm dG_{P,X}\{Q_P(X)\}=0\). Consequently \(Q_P\{\mathcal T_P(X,t)\}=Q_P(X)\) and \(P\{\mathcal T_P(X,t)\}=P(X)\) for every \(X\in S3\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\).
body.justification: This converts determinant singularity and symmetric-gradient integrability into exact finite translation invariance under the trace-pairing convention.
body.gap: De Bondt supplies a quasi-translation criterion, but does not derive the adjugate direction from a symmetric gradient or combine it with positive-cone order.
body.consumer: Theorem 2 transports a rank-two null direction along exact polynomial rays.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(G=G_P\) and \(Q=Q_P=\operatorname{adj}G\).  The trace pairing on \(S3\) is nondegenerate.  Because \(G\) is the gradient of \(P\), equality of the two second directional derivatives gives, for all \(H,J\in S3\),
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\!\left(\mathrm dG_X(H)J\right)
 =\mathrm d^2P_X(H,J)
 =\mathrm d^2P_X(J,H)
 =\operatorname{tr}\!\left(H\,\mathrm dG_X(J)\right).
\]
This identity uses the trace-pairing definition of \(G_P\); in ordinary coordinates it is exactly the convention that an off-diagonal coordinate derivative is twice the corresponding off-diagonal entry of \(G_P\).

Expanding the determinant by the Leibniz formula and differentiating each monomial shows, including at singular matrices, that its directional derivative at a matrix \(A\) in direction \(B\) is \(\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(A)B)\).  Applying this identity and the hypothesis \(\det G\equiv0\) gives, for arbitrary \(H\in S3\),
\[
 0=\mathrm d(\det G)_X(H)
  =\operatorname{tr}\!\left(Q(X)\,\mathrm dG_X(H)\right)
  =\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\mathrm dG_X(Q(X))H\right).
\]
Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing therefore gives
\[
 \mathrm dG_X(Q(X))=0. \tag{1}
\]
Let \(\mathcal L\) be the polynomial derivation \(\mathcal Lh(X)=\mathrm dh_X(Q(X))\), acting entrywise on matrix-valued polynomials.  Equation (1), the polynomial chain rule for the adjugate, and \(GQ=(\det G)I_3\) give
\[
 \mathcal LG=0,
 \qquad
 \mathcal LQ=\mathrm d(\operatorname{adj})_{G}(\mathcal LG)=0,
 \qquad
 \mathcal LP=\operatorname{tr}(GQ)=3\det G=0. \tag{2}
\]
For every scalar polynomial \(h\) and every integer \(k\geq0\), induction using \(\mathcal LQ=0\) yields
\[
 \mathcal L^kh(X)=\mathrm d^kh_X\bigl(Q(X),\ldots,Q(X)\bigr). \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, differentiating the right side along \(Q(X)\) gives its next directional derivative plus \(k\) terms containing \(\mathrm dQ_X(Q(X))=\mathcal LQ(X)=0\).  Apply (3) entrywise first to \(G\), and then to \(Q=\operatorname{adj}G\), or apply it directly with (2).  Since every derivative of order exceeding the polynomial degree vanishes, the finite Taylor formula and (2)--(3) give
\[
 G(X+tQ(X))=G(X),
 \qquad
 Q(X+tQ(X))=Q(X),
 \qquad
 P(X+tQ(X))=P(X)
\]
for every \(X\in S3\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\).  These are precisely the asserted identities for \(\mathcal T_P\).
